summary: Piperaquine is a long-acting bisquinoline antimalarial used as the partner drug in the artemisinin-based combination therapy dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ) for the treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, recommended by the WHO and approved in Europe (Eurartesim). It is not FDA-approved and is not used as monotherapy. It is dosed by body weight as a fixed-dose combination once daily for 3 days. Its principal safety concern is dose- and concentration-related QT-interval prolongation, so it should be given on an empty stomach (food increases absorption and QT risk) with attention to ECG/QTc, electrolytes and concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.
indications: Treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (as the partner drug in dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine artemisinin combination therapy)
WHO-recommended first- or second-line ACT for uncomplicated falciparum malaria where appropriate
Used in some settings for intermittent preventive/seasonal malaria chemoprevention per WHO guidance (combination)

dosage.c: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria (adult, fixed-dose with DHA)
dosage.d: Target ~18 mg/kg piperaquine (with ~4 mg/kg dihydroartemisinin) once daily for 3 days
dosage.n: Use the weight band of the fixed-dose tablet (e.g., Eurartesim/WHO)

dosage.d: e.g., 36 to <75 kg: 3 tablets (320 mg PPQ + 40 mg DHA) once daily for 3 days; 75 to <100 kg: 4 tablets once daily for 3 days
dosage.n: Follow the exact weight-band table in the product label

dosage.d: Same ~18 mg/kg/day piperaquine target using pediatric tablet strengths per weight band over 3 days
dosage.n: Minimum body weight per label (commonly >=5 kg)

dosage.d: Do not give a second course within ~2 months because of the long half-life and QT accumulation risk

admin: Give as the fixed-dose combination once daily at about the same time for 3 consecutive days
Take on an empty stomach with water - no food for at least 3 hours before and after each dose (food raises absorption and QT risk)
If vomiting occurs within 30 minutes, repeat the full dose; within 30-60 minutes, repeat half the dose
Complete the full 3-day course even if the patient feels better
Obtain a baseline ECG where QT risk factors exist and avoid co-administration with other QT-prolonging drugs
moa: Piperaquine is a bisquinoline that, like other 4-aminoquinoline-type antimalarials, accumulates in the parasite's acidic digestive (food) vacuole and inhibits the detoxifying polymerization of heme into inert hemozoin during hemoglobin digestion. The resulting accumulation of toxic free heme kills intra-erythrocytic Plasmodium. Its long half-life provides post-treatment prophylaxis and protects the rapidly acting artemisinin partner from resistance.

absolute: Congenital long QT syndrome / family history of sudden death from long QT
Known QT prolongation or clinically relevant cardiac arrhythmia / symptomatic bradycardia
Concomitant use of other QT-prolonging medicines
relative: Recent prior course of piperaquine (long half-life accumulation)
monitor: ECG / QTc interval (baseline and as indicated)

preg: Avoid in the first trimester; data are limited and artemisinins are generally avoided in early pregnancy. In the second and third trimesters use only if the benefit outweighs the risk and no suitable alternative exists, per WHO malaria-in-pregnancy guidance.
lact: Limited data exist on excretion into breast milk; given piperaquine's very long half-life, use with caution during breastfeeding and follow current WHO/SmPC advice.
renal: There are limited data in renal impairment; use with caution and avoid in significant impairment unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk, with attention to QT and electrolytes.
hepatic: Use with caution; avoid in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment because of altered metabolism and increased risk of QT-related effects, per the product label.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, ondansetron, methadone) - additive arrhythmia/QT risk; avoid
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir) - increase piperaquine exposure and QT risk
moderate: Drugs/conditions causing electrolyte disturbance (diuretics) - increase torsade risk
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin, certain anticonvulsants) - may reduce piperaquine levels and efficacy
minor: Piperaquine can mildly inhibit some CYP enzymes - clinical relevance usually limited
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach - fatty/food intake substantially increases piperaquine absorption and thereby the QT-prolongation risk; allow at least 3 hours fasting before and after each dose.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol during treatment; it offers no benefit and may add to cardiac and hepatic risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs the ECG QT/QTc interval; confirm malaria diagnosis (blood film/RDT) before and assess parasitemia after treatment.

serious: Torsades de pointes / serious ventricular arrhythmia
emergency: Palpitations, syncope or collapse (possible torsades de pointes)
Signs of severe allergic reaction (angioedema, breathing difficulty)
Features of severe/complicated malaria requiring parenteral therapy

monitoring: ECG / QTc, especially with cardiac risk factors or co-medication
Parasitemia and clinical/temperature response to confirm cure
Hemoglobin and signs of hemolysis or anemia
counsel: Take the full 3-day course exactly as directed, even once you feel better
Take each dose on an empty stomach with water - no food for 3 hours before and after
Tell your clinician about any heart rhythm problems, fainting, or other medicines, as this drug can affect the heart's rhythm
Report palpitations, fainting, severe dizziness, or yellowing of the skin/eyes promptly
If you vomit shortly after a dose, contact your provider about repeating it; return if fever or symptoms persist
pk: Antimalarial activity within the first day (with the artemisinin partner clearing parasites fast)
Plasma peak ~5 hours after an oral dose (increased by food)
Prolonged post-treatment prophylactic effect for several weeks
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture; in original packaging
pearls: Not FDA-approved; used as the WHO-recommended ACT partner drug in dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHA-PPQ) and approved in Europe as Eurartesim - this record uses WHO and EMA/SmPC references
KEY RISK: dose- and concentration-related QT prolongation - take on an EMPTY stomach (food raises absorption and QT risk) and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs
Dose is by body weight over 3 days as a fixed-dose combination; never used as monotherapy
Very long half-life (weeks) gives post-treatment prophylaxis but means a repeat course should not be given within ~2 months
Check electrolytes and consider a baseline ECG in patients with cardiac risk factors
missed: Doses are given once daily for 3 days. If a daily dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered the same day on an empty stomach; if a whole day is missed, contact the prescriber for advice rather than doubling up, and ensure all 3 daily doses are completed.
overdose: Overdose risks marked QT prolongation and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmia (torsades de pointes). There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with continuous ECG and cardiac monitoring (for at least the period of QT risk given the long half-life), correction of electrolytes, and standard treatment of arrhythmias. Contact a poison center.
